To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the template activity of calf-thymus DNA was decreased by U.V. laser exposure at 2650 Angstroms.
U.V. light from a laser at 2650 Angstroms causes damage to the template activity of DNA, and that U.V.-treated DNA inhibits the activity of non-treated DNA.
U.V. light at 2650A, delivered at a peak power of 10 to the 9th power Watts per square centimeter, causes a decrease in template activity of DNA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of U.V. laser irradiation on DNA.
a study of the effect of laser irradiation at 2650A on the template activity of DNA.
the effects of U.V. lasers on deoxyribnucleic acid and its possible use for gene therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the U.V. lasers are capable of inducing DNA damage and that these effects are qualitatively similar, but not quantitatively identical, to the effects induced by the conventional U.V. sources.
U.V. lasers at 2650A have no significant effect on DNA template activity at the power densities used.
U.V. lasers at 2650A have no effect on the molecular weight of DNA and that the observed effects are probably due to the absorption of the laser light by some other component in the sample.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the U.V. lasers can produce a variety of effects in DNA, but that the mechanism of action is different from that of conventional U.V.
the U.V. lasers are not a suitable tool for DNA studies because the high peak powers are not compatible with DNA and that the low power lasers would be required for DNA work.
the U.V. effects on DNA are not due to the U.V. light itself but to a chemical change in the DNA induced by U.V. light.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the U.V. lasers can be used as an alternative to conventional U.V. sources to inactivate DNA.
the U.V. lasers can be used to modify DNA without the need of a photosensitizer.
U.V. lasers can be used as a tool to probe the structure-function relationships in DNA.
